title: Keyboard geography and note names
summary: Name every white and black key, understand octaves, and measure half and whole steps.

lessons.title: The white keys: A to G
lessons.summary: Use the two- and three-black-key groups to name every white key.

steps.title: The musical alphabet
steps.body:
Music uses only seven letter names: **A B C D E F G**. After G, the letters start again at A.

On the piano, the white keys run through those letters from left to right. Starting from C, you get **C D E F G A B**, then C again.

- Around each **group of two black keys**: **C D E** (C left, D between, E right).
- Around each **group of three black keys**: **F G A B** (F left, G and A between, B right).

diagram.caption: C D E around two black keys; F G A B around three.

steps.title: Up the white keys from middle C
steps.caption: C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5. Each step goes one white key to the right.

exercise.prompt: Play the white keys from middle C up to the next C: C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5. Use any fingers for now; say each name out loud.

mistakeTips: D is the white key between the two black keys.
F is just left of the three black keys.
B is just left of the next C.

exercise.prompt: Find and play each note: F4, A4, D4, B4, E4, G4.

mistakeTips: F: left edge of the three-black-key group.
A: between the second and third black keys of the three-group.
E: right edge of the two-black-key group.

reviewItems.prompt: Which white keys surround the group of three black keys?
Play the A above middle C.

lessons.title: Octaves
lessons.summary: The same letter repeats every eight white keys; octave numbers tell you which one.

steps.title: Same letter, higher or lower
steps.body:
From one C to the next C is an **octave**: 8 white keys counting both Cs, or 12 keys counting white and black. Notes an octave apart share a letter name and sound alike, one higher and one lower.

In **scientific pitch notation**, the number changes at every C: B3 is followed by C4. So the white keys go … A3 B3 **C4** D4 … B4 **C5** …

- Lower pitch = further left. Higher pitch = further right.
- The piano runs from **A0** (lowest) to **C8** (highest).

diagram.caption: Three Gs, each an octave apart: G3, G4, G5.

steps.title: Octaves on G
steps.caption: G3, G4, G5. Same name, higher each time.

exercise.prompt: Play every F you can find in 40 seconds.

mistakeTips: F is the white key just left of each group of three black keys.
Work steadily from left to right so you do not skip one.
Notes at the far ends are harder for the microphone to hear; play them a little louder.

exercise.prompt: Play these exact notes: E3, E4, E5, then A3, A4.

mistakeTips: Start from middle C (C4). E4 is two white keys to its right.
The number changes at C: the E just below middle C is E3.
A3 is the A just below middle C; A4 is the A just above it.

questions.prompt: How many white keys from one C to the next C, counting both?
questions.explanation: C D E F G A B C: eight white keys. Counting black keys too, it is 12 half steps.

questions.prompt: Which note comes right after B3 on the white keys?
questions.explanation: Octave numbers change at C, so the next white key after B3 is C4.

questions.prompt: What is the lowest note on an 88-key piano?
questions.explanation: The keyboard starts on A0 and ends on C8.

choices: Share a letter name and sound alike
questions.explanation: An octave doubles the frequency, which is why the two notes blend.

reviewItems.prompt: Where does the octave number change?

lessons.title: Half steps and whole steps
lessons.summary: Measure distance on the keyboard in half steps and whole steps.

steps.title: The smallest step
steps.body:
A **half step** (also called a **semitone**) is the distance from one key to the very next key, black or white, with nothing in between.

- C to the black key right of it is a half step.
- **E to F** and **B to C** are half steps between two white keys: there is no black key between them.

A **whole step** (a **whole tone**) is two half steps: skip exactly one key. C to D is a whole step (skipping the black key). E to F♯ is a whole step.

diagram.caption: E–F and B–C: half steps with no black key between.

steps.title: Half step, then whole step
steps.caption: C4 to D♭4 (half step), then C4 to D4 (whole step).

exercise.prompt: Play the chromatic scale (every key, black and white, in half steps) from middle C to the next C, 13 keys: C4 C♯4 D4 D♯4 E4 F4 F♯4 G4 G♯4 A4 A♯4 B4 C5.

mistakeTips: Every key, black and white, in order: no skipping.
E4 goes straight to F4; there is no black key between.
Use fingers 2 and 3 of your right hand, alternating, if that is comfortable.

questions.prompt: Which pair is a half step apart?
questions.explanation: E–F has no black key between it, so it is one half step. The others are whole steps.
A whole step skips exactly one key.

questions.prompt: Which pair of white keys is a whole step apart?
questions.explanation: G–A has a black key between it, so it is two half steps.

questions.prompt: How many half steps are in an octave?
questions.explanation: Counting every key from C to the next C gives 12 half steps.

reviewItems.prompt: Which two pairs of white keys are only a half step apart?

lessons.title: Sharps, flats, and the black keys
lessons.summary: Name black keys with sharps and flats, and meet enharmonic notes.

steps.title: Sharp and flat
steps.body:
- A **sharp (♯)** raises a note by a half step. The black key just right of C is **C♯**.
- A **flat (♭)** lowers a note by a half step. The black key just left of D is **D♭**.

That is the same key, so it has two names: **C♯ = D♭**. Two names for the same pitch are called **enharmonic** spellings. The five black keys in each octave are:

**C♯/D♭, D♯/E♭, F♯/G♭, G♯/A♭, A♯/B♭**

Which name to use depends on the key and the chord (you will learn this in later stages). In this app, sharps are written with # and flats with b in note names like F#4 or Bb3.

diagram.caption: The five black keys, named with sharps.

steps.title: Sharps and flats on white keys
steps.body: Because E–F and B–C are half steps, a sharp or flat can land on a white key: **E♯ = F**, **B♯ = C**, **F♭ = E**, **C♭ = B**. These spellings are rare, but they do appear in music with many sharps or flats.

steps.title: One key, two names
steps.caption: F♯4, then G♭4: the same key and the same sound.

exercise.prompt: Play these black keys: F♯4, B♭4, C♯4, E♭4, G♯4, A♭3.

mistakeTips: F♯ is the first black key of the three-group.
B♭ is the last black key of the three-group (just left of B).
C♯ is the first black key of the two-group; E♭ is the second.
A♭3 is the same key as G♯3, just below middle C.

choices: Raises a note by a half step
Lowers a note by a half step
Raises a note by a whole step
questions.explanation: Sharp = up one half step; flat = down one half step.

questions.prompt: Which is another name for D♯?
questions.explanation: The black key between D and E is D♯ or E♭.

questions.prompt: Which is another name for G♭?
questions.explanation: The black key between F and G is F♯ or G♭.

questions.prompt: B♯ is played on which key?
questions.explanation: B–C is a half step, so raising B by a half step lands on C.

reviewItems.prompt: Give both names for the black key between A and B.

branches.title: Reading the grand staff
branches.summary: Read notes in the treble and bass clefs and connect them to keys on the piano.

lessons.title: The treble clef
lessons.summary: Lines and spaces of the treble staff, usually played by the right hand.

steps.title: The staff
steps.body:
Written music uses a **staff**: five horizontal lines with four spaces between them. Each line and each space is one white-key letter. Moving up one line-or-space moves up one letter.

A **clef** at the start of the staff tells you which notes the lines mean. The **treble clef** (𝄞) curls around the second line from the bottom, which is **G4**; that is why it is also called the G clef.

diagram.caption: Treble clef: the curl circles G4.

steps.title: Lines and spaces
steps.body:
- **Lines**, bottom to top: **E4 G4 B4 D5 F5**, often remembered as "Every Good Boy Does Fine."
- **Spaces**, bottom to top: **F4 A4 C5 E5**, which spell **FACE**.
- **Middle C (C4)** sits on a short extra line just below the staff, called a **ledger line**.

steps.title: Treble staff, bottom line to top line
steps.caption: E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 F5: line, space, line, space…

exercise.prompt: Read each note on the staff and play it: G4, E4, C5, F4, D5, A4.

mistakeTips: Lines: E G B D F. Spaces: F A C E.
Count up from a note you know, such as G4 on the second line.
C5 is the third space, one octave above middle C.

reviewItems.prompt: Treble clef lines, bottom to top?
Treble clef spaces, bottom to top?

lessons.title: The bass clef
lessons.summary: Lines and spaces of the bass staff, usually played by the left hand.

steps.title: The bass clef
steps.body:
The **bass clef** (𝄢) marks lower notes. Its two dots sit on either side of the fourth line from the bottom, which is **F3**; that is why it is also called the F clef.

- **Lines**, bottom to top: **G2 B2 D3 F3 A3**, often remembered as "Good Boys Do Fine Always."
- **Spaces**, bottom to top: **A2 C3 E3 G3**, "All Cows Eat Grass."
- **Middle C (C4)** sits on a ledger line just **above** the bass staff.

diagram.caption: Bass clef: the dots surround F3.

steps.title: Bass staff, bottom line to top line
steps.caption: G2 A2 B2 C3 D3 E3 F3 G3 A3.

exercise.prompt: Read each bass-clef note and play it with your left hand: F3, C3, A3, G2, E3, D3.

mistakeTips: Lines: G B D F A. Spaces: A C E G.
F3 is the line between the two dots of the clef.
C3 is the second space, one octave below middle C.
G2 is low; play it firmly so the microphone catches it.

reviewItems.prompt: Bass clef lines, bottom to top?
Bass clef spaces, bottom to top?

lessons.title: The grand staff and landmark notes
lessons.summary: Join the two clefs, read from landmarks, and read accidentals on the staff.

steps.title: One staff for two hands
steps.body:
Piano music uses the **grand staff**: a treble staff above a bass staff, joined by a brace. Usually the right hand reads the top staff and the left hand reads the bottom staff.

Middle C is the link: it is one ledger line below the treble staff **and** one ledger line above the bass staff. Both are the same key, C4.

diagram.caption: Middle C sits between the two staves.

steps.title: Landmark notes
steps.body:
Instead of counting from the bottom every time, learn a few **landmarks** and read by step from them:

- **Treble G4** (second line, where the clef curls)
- **Treble C5** (third space)
- **Middle C4** (ledger line between the staves)
- **Bass F3** (fourth line, between the clef's dots)
- **Bass C3** (second space)

A note on the next line up from a line note is a **skip** (two letters, such as G to B). A note in the space just above a line is a **step** (one letter).

steps.title: Accidentals on the staff
steps.body:
A sharp (♯) or flat (♭) placed before a note applies to that note **for the rest of the measure** (the bar). A **natural sign (♮)** cancels it and returns to the white key.

At the start of each line you may also see a **key signature**: sharps or flats that apply to every note of that letter throughout the piece. You will use key signatures in Stage 6.

exercise.prompt: Landmark drill: play C3 (left hand), F3 (left hand), C4, G4 (right hand), C5 (right hand).

mistakeTips: C3 is the second space of the bass staff.
F3 sits between the bass clef's dots.
G4 is where the treble clef curls.

reviewItems.prompt: Where is middle C on the grand staff?
reviewItems.answer: On a ledger line between the staves: below the treble staff and above the bass staff.

reviewItems.prompt: How long does an accidental last?
reviewItems.answer: Until the end of the measure (bar line), unless cancelled by a natural sign.
